cards.body: You're offside if you're nearer the goal than both the ball and the second-last defender when the ball is played to you. Key exceptions: no offside from a goal kick, throw-in, or corner — and never in your own half. It's about timing the run, not standing still.
cards.title: Offside, finally explained

cards.body: Goalkeeper: shot-stopper and sweeper. Defenders: win duels, protect the box. Midfielders: control tempo, link play. Forwards: create and finish chances. Modern players blur the lines — full-backs attack, strikers press — but the jobs stay the same.
cards.title: Four lines, four jobs

cards.body: Think in thirds: defensive third (safety first), middle third (control and build), final third (creativity and risk). Great teams play out from the back through the thirds instead of launching it long and hoping.
Beginners watch the ball. Learn to watch the team's shape instead: the distances between lines, the width, the compactness. You'll suddenly see why attacks die — the shape broke before the pass did.

choices: Receiving the ball in their own half
Standing beyond the last defender as the ball is played
Getting the ball from a throw-in
cards.explain: No offside in your own half, ever — and none from throw-ins either. Beyond the last defender when the ball is played is the classic flag.
cards.q: When is a player NOT offside?

choices: Yes — level with the defender is onside
questions.explain: Level is onside. Offside needs the attacker BEYOND the second-last defender when the ball is played.
questions.q: A striker times his run behind the defense as the pass is played. Legal?

questions.explain: Throw-ins, corners, and goal kicks are offside-free. Through balls and crosses are judged normally.
questions.q: No offside can be given from…

choices: Control tempo and link defense to attack
questions.explain: Midfielders are the connectors — they dictate rhythm and bridge the lines.

choices: To build through the thirds with control
questions.explain: Playing through the thirds keeps possession and drags opponents out of shape. Hoofing it surrenders the ball.
questions.q: Why do teams 'play out from the back'?

choices: Watch the team's shape, not just the ball
questions.explain: Shape reveals everything — compactness, width, broken lines. The ball just follows the shape.
questions.q: Best habit for reading a match?

flashcards.back: Nearer the goal than ball + second-last defender when the ball is played = offside.
Keeper, defenders, midfielders, forwards — each with a distinct job.
Defensive, middle, final — teams build play through them in order.
Distances between lines and width — watch it instead of the ball.

cards.body: 4-3-3 (four defenders, three mids, three forwards) screams attack: wide wingers stretch the pitch. 4-4-2 is compact and direct: two banks of four, two strikers up top. Formation is just the starting shape — what players DO in it is the tactic.
cards.title: 4-3-3 vs 4-4-2: shape is a statement

cards.body: Pressing means hunting the ball high up the pitch the moment you lose it — gegenpressing wants it back within seconds. It needs insane fitness and coordination: one lazy presser and the whole trap collapses.
cards.title: Pressing: defend by attacking

cards.body: Barcelona's tiki-taka: short, quick passes, constant movement, keep the ball until the defense falls asleep — then strike. It demands elite technique from all eleven. Possession isn't the point; the chance at the end is.
Sit deep, stay compact, invite pressure — then explode forward into the space they left behind. Pace up front is non-negotiable. It's the underdog's superpower and every giant's nightmare.

choices: The whole team hunting together, instantly
cards.explain: Pressing is collective — eleven players squeezing space as one. A solo chase just opens gaps.

questions.explain: The 4-3-3 stretches play wide with three forwards — it's built to attack.
questions.q: A team lines up 4-3-3. What should you expect?

choices: The chance at the end of the possession
questions.explain: Possession is the setup, not the point. All those passes exist to manufacture one killer opening.
Pressing commits bodies forward. If the trap fails, the space behind is wide open.
questions.q: Why does a failed press get punished?

choices: Pace up front to exploit space
questions.explain: Counters live on speed — fast players sprinting into the acres the opponent vacated.

choices: Formation is the shape; tactics are what players do in it
questions.explain: 4-3-3 on paper means little. The pressing triggers, rotations, and patterns are the actual tactic.

flashcards.back: Attacking shape: wide wingers stretch the pitch, three mids control the middle.
Win the ball back within seconds of losing it — defend by attacking.
Short quick passes and movement; possession with a killer final ball.
Absorb pressure deep, then explode into the space behind.

cards.body: The half-space is the channel between the wing and the center — too wide for center-backs, too central for full-backs. Playmakers live here: De Bruyne, Özil, and yes — Messi. Receive between the lines in the half-space and the defense has no good answer.
cards.title: The half-space: football's cheat code

cards.body: Player A passes to B — but the REAL threat is C, sprinting past both into space. Defenders track the ball and the receiver; nobody tracks the third man. It's the most underrated pattern in football — watch for the runner, not the pass.
cards.title: Third-man runs break lines

cards.body: Messi starts wide right, then drifts inside onto his left foot — cutting into the half-space where he can shoot, slide a through ball, or combine. The full-back can't follow without abandoning the wing; the center-back can't step out without opening the middle. One drift, two defenders frozen.

The ball is a magnet for eyes — and defenders. The danger usually develops on the FAR side: the winger's blind run, the late midfielder arriving. Train your eyes away from the ball and you'll predict goals before they happen.

choices: It sits between defenders' zones — nobody owns it
It's the closest spot to the goal
cards.explain: Too wide for the center-back, too central for the full-back. Receive there and the defense must choose who breaks shape.
cards.q: Why is the half-space so dangerous?

choices: No defender owns that zone without breaking shape
questions.explain: Stepping out opens a gap; staying lets him turn. The half-space forces a lose-lose choice.
questions.q: A playmaker receives between the lines in the half-space. Why is the defense stuck?

choices: Often the third man — the untracked runner
questions.explain: Defenses track ball and receiver. The third man's run arrives unmarked — that's the design.
questions.q: In a third-man combination, who scores?

choices: Enter the half-space on his left foot
questions.explain: Inside he's a triple threat — shoot, through ball, or combine — with two defenders frozen by the dilemma.
questions.q: Messi drifts inside from the right wing mainly to…

choices: Watch the far side, away from the ball
questions.explain: The ball hypnotizes defenders and viewers alike. The far-side run is where the danger brews.
questions.q: Best way to predict an attack?

choices: In the gap between midfield and defense
questions.explain: That pocket of space is where the number 10s live — turn there and you face a retreating defense.

flashcards.back: The channel between wing and center — the playmaker's paradise.
The runner beyond the passer and receiver — the one nobody tracks.
Receiving in the gap between midfield and defense.
Blind-side run away from the ball — where goals are born.
